design_detail: Within-person laboratory study in 10 healthy volunteers, described by the authors as placebo-controlled and counterbalanced, with brain imaging. Each person had three [18F]fluorodeoxyglucose PET scans a month apart: a baseline (placebo) scan, an (S)-ketamine scan and an (R)-ketamine scan. In each drug scan an induction amount of 15 mg of the enantiomer in 20 ml saline was given intravenously over 5 min, followed by 5 min with no further supply and then a continuous intravenous infusion at 0.014-0.02 mg/kg/min for 53 min; the (R)-ketamine condition was equimolar to the (S)-ketamine condition (pp. 26-27). Psychopathology was rated with the APZ, AMDP, EPI and EWL scales, cerebral glucose metabolism (CMRglu) was measured in 18 regions of interest per hemisphere placed on Talairach coordinates, and arterial plasma ketamine was measured by gas chromatography-mass spectrometry at five time points. All comparisons used Wilcoxon matched-pairs tests and Spearman correlations with no correction for multiplicity.
can_establish: Whether, in 10 healthy volunteers acting as their own controls, a subanesthetic intravenous infusion of (S)-ketamine changes psychopathology ratings and regional brain glucose metabolism relative to a placebo scan, and whether an equimolar (R)-ketamine infusion does the same; and how the two enantiomer conditions compare within the same people.
cannot_establish: Which specific brain change produces which symptom (correlations with n=10 and no multiplicity correction, as the authors say); whether the effects were observed under maintained blinding (every participant had already received (S)-ketamine in a preliminary session and the authors state that all of them recognised the (R)-ketamine condition as a drug effect, pp. 28, 36); anything about repeated or longer-term use, about people who use ketamine outside the laboratory, about racemic ketamine as sold, or about people with psychiatric illness; and whether any change outlasts the session, since all measurements were made during or immediately after the infusion.

sample.recruitment: Not stated beyond the setting: volunteers examined at the Research Department of the Psychiatric University Hospital Zurich, the MRI Center of the University Hospital of Zurich and the PET Department of the Paul Scherrer Institute, Villigen. No advertisement, register or referral route is described (p. 26).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Healthy volunteers screened by psychiatric interview for absence of personal and first-degree family history of major psychiatric disorder; anyone with a history of non-medical use of illicit drugs was excluded (the paper uses the older term); the openness and neuroticism scales of the Freiburg Personality Inventory were also used as exclusion criteria; physical examination, electrocardiogram, blood and urine analysis normal, and a normal MRI (p. 26).
sample.demographics: 10 volunteers, 6 men and 4 women, mean age 30.4 years (Table 1 ages 24-42). Table 1 gives each person's FPI openness (mean 7.9, SD 3.1) and neuroticism (mean 3.5, SD 2.2) against sex- and age-matched normative means printed in the table footnote (openness 6.79 +/- 2.79 men, 6.05 +/- 2.87 women; neuroticism 5.52 +/- 3.52 men, 6.73 +/- 3.65 women). No education, occupation, tobacco, alcohol or caffeine data (pp. 26-27).
sample.attrition: None reported: all 10 are listed in Table 1 with scores in all conditions, and no withdrawal is mentioned although participants were free to withdraw at any time (pp. 26-27).
sample.selection_effects: A small, screened, psychiatrically and physically healthy volunteer sample at a university hospital, deliberately selected for low openness and neuroticism scores and for absence of non-medical drug use, and prepared by a preliminary (S)-ketamine session. Effects in such a group need not transfer to people who use ketamine outside the laboratory, to people with psychiatric illness, or to people taking other drugs; and a sample conditioned by a prior drug exposure session will have different expectations from a drug-naive one.

exposure.measurement: Drug given and measured in the laboratory: arterial plasma ketamine by a gas chromatography-mass spectrometry method with a stated sensitivity of 10 ng/ml, sampled through the radial artery cannula at 0, 10, 30, 48 and 54 min; samples stored at -20 degrees C (p. 29). The enantiomers were prepared by the Department of Pharmacology, University of Oslo and dissolved in 0.9% sterile NaCl at 1 mg/ml each (p. 27).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only, as printed: intravenously, 15 mg of (S)- or (R)-ketamine in 20 ml saline over 5 min as an induction step, then 5 min with no further supply, then a continuous infusion at 0.014-0.02 mg/kg/min for 53 min, by infusion pump; the (R)-ketamine condition was equimolar to the (S)-ketamine condition, and the (S)-ketamine condition was described as 60% of the racemic amount used in the authors' earlier study. One exposure per condition, three conditions a month apart (pp. 26-27).
exposure.polysubstance: Not addressed: no concurrent medication, tobacco, alcohol or caffeine use is reported, and nothing is said about what participants consumed on scan days. The only other drug exposure described is the preliminary (S)-ketamine session before the PET phase (p. 28).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not reported. No pre-scan toxicology or abstinence requirement is described; scans were a month apart, and arrival at the PET department was at 1100 h (p. 28).

comparison.controls: Each participant's own baseline (placebo) PET scan, and the other enantiomer condition in the same person. No separate control group and no group of people with psychiatric illness.
comparison.matching: Within-person design; the three scans were counterbalanced at monthly intervals. No randomisation method, sequence generation or allocation concealment is described, and no period or carryover effect is modelled (p. 26).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable in the usual sense, because each person is their own baseline. What is unmeasured is expectancy: every participant had already experienced (S)-ketamine in the preliminary session, no measure of what participants believed they had received is reported, and the placebo scan is a single occasion with no test of whether people could tell it apart from the drug scans.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Not applicable (no separate control group). Participants' own use of other substances is not reported.

outcomes.instruments: Psychopathology, rated for the phase during the PET scan: the Altered States of Consciousness questionnaire (APZ), a self-report giving a global score and three subscale scores, oceanic boundlessness (OSE, derealisation and depersonalisation with positive mood), dread of ego-dissolution (AIA, ego-disintegration, loss of autonomy, anxiety, paranoid feelings) and visionary restructuralization (VUS, illusions, pseudo-hallucinations and hallucinations, changes in the meaning of percepts); the Ego Pathology Inventory (EPI), rated by a psychiatrist, giving a global score and five subscales (ego identity, demarcation, consistency, activity, vitality); the AMDP inventory, giving syndrome scores for schizophrenia and manic-depression and 12 subscales including apathy, hallucinatory-disintegration and thought disorder; and the EWL self-rated mood scale with seven scales (efficiency, deactivation, extroversion, introversion, well-being, irritability, anxiety). Imaging: [18F]FDG PET on a CTI Siemens 933/04-16 tomograph, 8 mm in-plane resolution, 12 planes, mean administered FDG dose 177.6 MBq (min 107.3, max 244.2), 23 arterial samples, autoradiographic method of Rhodes et al., images transformed to Talairach space, standardised regions of interest (5.6-10.4 mm) drawn symmetrically in both hemispheres; absolute CMRglu in micromol per 100 g per min, relative CMRglu (region divided by whole-brain mean) and metabolic gradients (ratios between two regions in the same hemisphere) (pp. 27-29).
outcomes.validity_norms: The APZ dimensions are said to have been derived and validated in an international study of altered states and to be independent of what induced the state; the EPI is cited as a validated measure of ego pathology; FPI normative means for healthy controls are printed in the Table 1 footnote. No norms are given for the AMDP or EWL, and no reliability figures for any rating in this study. The PET method is standard for its time but regional values are hand-placed standardised regions of interest, not voxelwise statistics.
outcomes.operationalization: No outcome is operationalised as harm or impairment. The psychosis-like state is operationalised as changes from the baseline scan in self-rated and psychiatrist-rated scale scores; hyperfrontality is operationalised as an increase in absolute and relative frontal CMRglu and an increase in fronto-occipital and fronto-temporal ratios, the ratio method being taken from published work on people with schizophrenia.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None, and the authors say so: with no correction for the number of comparisons the results should be regarded as exploratory rather than confirmatory (p. 29). The count of about 180 is the editors' tally of the comparisons actually displayed or reported: 32 regional absolute CMRglu tests per enantiomer condition (Figs. 4 and 5), whole-brain tests, the relative CMRglu values reported in the text, 32 metabolic-ratio tests (Table 2, 8 ratios by 2 hemispheres by 2 conditions), about 34 psychopathology comparisons (Figs. 1 and 2) and about 45 correlations. The true number of comparisons made is larger, because 18 regions per hemisphere were measured and only 16 are plotted.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Participants are stated to have been blind to the drug conditions (p. 26); no blinding of the examining psychiatrist, of the person placing the regions of interest or of the analysts is reported. The Discussion states that participants could tell the (R)-ketamine condition from the placebo condition and that all of them correctly identified it as a drug effect, so blinding did not hold (pp. 34, 36).

analysis.effect_sizes: None reported: results are percentage changes from baseline with Wilcoxon P-levels, and correlations given only as P-levels with a sign. No confidence intervals, no standardised effect sizes, no test statistics. Dispersion is shown only in figures (mean and standard error bars in Figs. 1, 2, 4 and 5) and in Table 1 for the global scores. Editors' calculations from the per-person values in Table 1 (p. 27): the within-person difference between the (S)- and (R)-ketamine conditions in APZ global score is 22.6 points (SD 6.3; 95% CI 18.1 to 27.1; standardised paired difference about 3.6) and in EPI global score 23.3 points (SD 10.9; 95% CI 15.5 to 31.1; standardised paired difference about 2.1), with every one of the 10 participants higher under (S)-ketamine (exact two-sided sign test P = 0.002).
analysis.covariates: None. Unadjusted within-person comparisons; relative CMRglu and ratios are used instead of covariate adjustment to handle global and between-person variation in metabolism (pp. 28-29).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol, registration or pre-specified primary outcome. One a priori hypothesis is named, that (S)-ketamine would increase frontal CMRglu; everything else is described by the authors as exploratory (p. 29).
analysis.selective_reporting: Substantial. Of 18 regions per hemisphere, 16 are plotted and only some are given numerically in the text. Relative CMRglu values are reported for the regions that changed and not for the rest. Correlations are reported selectively: Table 2 shows only 8 of the many possible ratios, correlations with absolute CMRglu appear only in the text, and one result is given as data not shown (p. 36). Several values appear only in figures, from which exact numbers cannot be read.
analysis.power: Not reported; no sample-size calculation. With 10 participants and paired non-parametric tests the smallest attainable two-sided P is 0.002, so single P-values below 0.01 carry little information about size; the authors attribute several null correlations to the small sample (pp. 35-36).

interpretation_gap.results_show: In 10 healthy volunteers, an (S)-ketamine infusion at the stated rates produced a short-lived psychosis-like state (higher APZ, AMDP and EPI scores than the baseline scan) together with higher glucose metabolism across most of the brain, largest in frontal and cingulate cortex and smallest in posterior and subcortical regions, so that fronto-temporal and fronto-occipital ratios rose. An equimolar (R)-ketamine infusion in the same people produced no psychotic symptoms but a state of relaxation, with a general tendency to lower metabolism that reached significance only in the temporomedial cortex bilaterally and the left insula. The correlations between symptom scores and regional metabolism are exploratory, uncorrected, and based on 10 people.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract states that the metabolic changes in frontal and left temporal cortex correlated with ego-disintegration and hallucinatory phenomena, and that the (S)-ketamine-induced hyperfrontality appears to parallel findings in people with acute schizophrenic psychosis (p. 25). Two steps go beyond the data. First, the correlation claims rest on uncorrected tests in 10 people, reported as P-levels only, so neither their size nor their robustness can be judged; the authors themselves call the analysis exploratory (p. 29) and attribute non-significant correlations to the small sample (pp. 35-36). Second, the comparison with schizophrenia is made against published studies, not against patients studied here; the discussion is explicit that ego-pathology scores were about two-thirds of those reported for people with first-episode schizophrenia and that ego-activity and ego-vitality were clearly less affected (p. 34). The conclusion that (S)-ketamine is the predominant psychotomimetically active agent in racemic ketamine (p. 34) rests on a comparison with a different sample in the companion paper, not on a racemic condition tested here.

timeline.event: Krystal et al. report dose-related perceptual, cognitive and psychotomimetic effects of subanesthetic ketamine in healthy volunteers; cited here as the comparison for the symptom profile

Lahti et al. report that ketamine given to people with schizophrenia stabilized on haloperidol raised frontomedial and anterior cingulate blood flow with an exacerbation of positive symptoms (as cited in this paper, p. 36; not appraised here)
Companion paper from the same laboratory, in a different sample of 10 healthy volunteers, finds the same hyperfrontal pattern with racemic ketamine and larger whole-brain increases
The same group reports a [11C]raclopride PET study of striatal dopamine under (S)-ketamine (listed in the project source list as Vollenweider et al. 2000, J Psychiatr Res; not read here)

A meta-analysis of functional neuroimaging studies of ketamine in healthy volunteers is listed in the project source list (Ait Bentaleb et al.) and has not yet been appraised; it is the place to check whether the hyperfrontality finding holds across methods

replication.where_it_stands: The psychopathological contrast between the two enantiomer conditions is the paper's most robust result: it is within-person, in the same direction in all 10 participants, and large. The metabolic findings for (S)-ketamine agree with the same laboratory's racemic study in a different sample, which is consistency within one group rather than independent replication. The enantiomer comparison of cerebral glucose metabolism itself has not, as far as this reading shows, been repeated anywhere; later imaging work used different tracers and methods, and whether the hyperfrontality finding holds up across methods is a question for the neuroimaging meta-analysis on the project list, not yet appraised.

funding.funder: Supported in part by the Swiss National Science Research Foundation (32-32418.91) and Lundbeck Ltd, Switzerland (p. 37).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement appears in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: University and national-laboratory setting (Psychiatric University Hospital Zurich; Paul Scherrer Institute; University of Oslo, which prepared the enantiomers). Lundbeck Ltd is a pharmaceutical company; this is recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results. One author (I. Oye) is from the Oslo pharmacology department whose earlier work on the enantiomers supplies the receptor-affinity rationale for the study.

what_would_settle_it: A larger within-person study with a maintained and tested blind (participants and raters asked what they believed they received, with guessing reported), randomised order with period effects modelled, a pre-specified primary outcome and a correction for multiplicity, ideally with a racemic condition included in the same people so that the enantiomer comparison does not depend on a different sample, and with the imaging analysed voxelwise so that regional claims do not rest on hand-placed regions of interest.

domains.domain: Randomization process (order of the three conditions)
domains.note: Order is described only as counterbalanced at monthly intervals; no sequence generation, no allocation concealment and no statement of who assigned the order (p. 26).

Scans were a month apart, which makes pharmacological carryover unlikely, but no period or order effect is modelled or reported, and every participant had had a preliminary (S)-ketamine session before the PET phase (p. 28), so psychological carryover into the placebo and (R)-ketamine conditions cannot be excluded.

Participants are said to have been blind to the conditions, but the Discussion reports that they could distinguish the (R)-ketamine condition from placebo and that all of them correctly identified it as a drug effect (pp. 34, 36); with a prior drug-exposure session the (S)-ketamine condition cannot have been blind either. The self-rated APZ and EWL scores and the psychiatrist's ratings were therefore made in an effectively unblinded condition.
All 10 participants appear in Table 1 with scores in every condition and in the PET analyses; no missing data are reported.

PET quantification is objective, but regions of interest were placed by hand on standardised coordinates with no stated blinding and no reliability data. The psychopathology ratings are partly retrospective: the APZ and EWL were completed after drug effects had completely subsided and refer to the scan period, while the AMDP and EPI were rated immediately after the scan (p. 28).

No protocol and one named a priori hypothesis, with about 180 displayed comparisons and no multiplicity correction; regions, relative values, ratios and correlations are reported selectively, one correlation is given as data not shown (p. 36), and several values exist only in figures.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: As a within-person comparison of two enantiomer conditions against a placebo scan the design is strong, and the psychopathological contrast between (S)- and (R)-ketamine is large, consistent across all 10 participants and unlikely to be an artefact of the ratings alone. The overall judgment is set by the failure of blinding, which the authors themselves describe, and by the selective reporting of a large number of uncorrected comparisons. The source can be cited for: the psychopathological and metabolic profile of a subanesthetic (S)-ketamine infusion at the stated rates in healthy volunteers; the contrast with an equimolar (R)-ketamine infusion; plasma concentrations during such an infusion; and the pattern of regional glucose-metabolic change. It cannot be cited for the size of any symptom-metabolism association, for a causal statement about which brain region produces which symptom, for any claim about racemic ketamine as sold, or for any equivalence between this state and schizophrenia.

key_findings.finding: Ten healthy volunteers (male=6, female=4), mean age 30.4 years, each had three FDG-PET scans a month apart in counterbalanced order: a baseline (placebo) scan, an (S)-ketamine scan and an equimolar (R)-ketamine scan, with participants described as blind to the conditions.
key_findings.locator: Materials and method, Subjects (2.1) and Experimental design (2.2)

key_findings.finding: In each drug scan the enantiomer was given intravenously as 15 mg in 20 ml saline over 5 min, then 5 min with no further supply, then a continuous infusion at 0.014-0.02 mg/kg/min for 53 min; the (S)-ketamine amount is described as 60% of the racemic amount used in the authors' earlier study, and the (R)-ketamine condition as equimolar to it.
key_findings.locator: Materials and method, Experimental design (2.2), last paragraph (p. 26) continuing on p. 27

key_findings.finding: Plasma levels ranged from 269 to 523 ng/ml (mean 379, SD 71) in the (S)-ketamine condition and from 280 to 508 ng/ml (mean 389, SD 74) in the (R)-ketamine condition; psychotic symptoms appeared about 5 min after the start of the (S)-ketamine infusion at a mean plasma level of 539 ng/ml.
key_findings.note: The 539 ng/ml at symptom onset lies above the top of the stated (S)-ketamine range of 269-523 ng/ml; the paper does not reconcile the two, and does not say whether the range refers to per-person means of the five samples. The two conditions are described as equimolar, but no molar calculation, salt form or concentration check is printed beyond 1 mg/ml in 0.9% NaCl (p. 27), so these measured plasma levels are the only evidence that the two conditions were comparable.

key_findings.finding: (S)-ketamine produced depersonalisation and derealisation, visual disturbances from pseudohallucinations to complex hallucinations, thought disorder and apathy; auditory changes were illusions rather than true hallucinations. Reported emotional reactions were heightened feelings or euphoria in 30%, indifference in 30% and heightened anxiety in 40%. EWL mood scores rose for deactivation (P<0.01), introversion (P<0.05), emotional irritability (P<0.05) and anxiety (P<0.01).

Equimolar (R)-ketamine produced no psychotic symptoms in the same people but a state of relaxation: the APZ oceanic-boundlessness score rose only at trend level (P<0.06), EWL well-being at P<0.09 and emotional irritation fell at P<0.08.

Per-person global scores (Table 1): under (S)-ketamine the APZ global score ran from 25 to 55 and the EPI global score from 10 to 48, against 8 to 33 and 0 to 5 under (R)-ketamine. Editors' calculation from those 10 pairs: the within-person (S) minus (R) difference is 22.6 points (SD 6.3) for APZ global and 23.3 points (SD 10.9) for EPI global, higher under (S)-ketamine in every participant (exact two-sided sign test P = 0.002).
key_findings.locator: Table 1, columns S-Ketamine APZ/EPI global and R-Ketamine APZ/EPI global
key_findings.note: The printed mean and SD for the S-ketamine APZ global column (37.0, 12.6) do not match the 10 values above them, which give 38.2 and 10.3 (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: (S)-ketamine increased absolute CMRglu across most regions, with a front-to-back gradient: frontomedial 19.6%, frontolateral 20.1%, cingulate anterior 23.5%, cingulate posterior 24.0% and parietal 27.35% bilaterally; somatosensory 21.1% and motor 23.0% significantly in the left hemisphere only; the thalamus was the only subcortical region with a bilateral increase, at trend level (17%, P<0.07); whole-brain metabolism rose 12% but not significantly (P<0.09). Cortical regions were about 2-3 times more stimulated than subcortical regions and frontal regions about twice as much as posterior ones.
key_findings.locator: Results, Absolute and relative cerebral metabolic rates of glucose (3.3), 1st paragraph (p. 29) continuing on p. 31; Fig. 4 (p. 32)

key_findings.finding: Relative CMRglu (region divided by whole brain) rose bilaterally in the frontomedial (7.7%), frontolateral (8.4%) and cingulate posterior (12.5%) cortex and in the left parietal cortex (18.2%), and fell in the left temporomedial cortex (4.8%), all at P<0.05.
key_findings.locator: Results, Absolute and relative cerebral metabolic rates of glucose (3.3), 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: (R)-ketamine tended to lower CMRglu across regions: whole-brain -9.8% (P<0.07, not significant); significant absolute decreases bilaterally in the temporomedial cortex (-13.4%) and in the left insula (-14%); relative decreases in the right temporal cortex (-4.0%, P<0.05) and bilaterally in the cerebellum (-5.0% and -4.0%, P<0.05). Decreases in the cerebellum and left caudate-putamen reached only P<0.07.
key_findings.locator: Results, Absolute and relative cerebral metabolic rates of glucose (3.3), 2nd paragraph (p. 31); Fig. 5 (p. 33)

key_findings.finding: Metabolic gradients under (S)-ketamine (Table 2): fronto-temporal ratios rose between 6.8% and 14.0% and fronto-occipital ratios between 9.1% and 11.7%, with the left frontolateral-caudate ratio up 16.0%, the right frontomedial-putamen ratio up 12.3% and the right frontolateral-putamen ratio up 13.2%. Under (R)-ketamine the same ratios rose only 0.1% to 7.4%.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, columns Change of gradients (%) for S-Ketamine and R-Ketamine
key_findings.note: Significance varies by row and hemisphere: of the fronto-occipital ratios only the left frontolateral-occipitolateral change is marked P<0.05, the left frontomedial-occipitomedial change is trend level and both right-hemisphere changes are marked not significant.

key_findings.finding: Correlations with absolute CMRglu under (S)-ketamine, all uncorrected and in the whole sample of ten: APZ oceanic boundlessness with frontomedial cortex (left P<0.05, right P<0.07) and right temporomedial cortex (P<0.05); EPI ego-identity impairment with frontomedial (P<0.04/P<0.04), frontolateral (P<0.05/P<0.04), cingulate anterior (P<0.01/P<0.004) and right cingulate posterior (P<0.04) cortex; APZ visionary restructuralization and AMDP hallucinatory-disintegration with occipitomedial (P<0.07/P<0.06) and occipitolateral (P<0.06/P<0.05) cortex; AMDP apathy with both parietal cortices (P<0.01/P<0.04) and the left insula (P<0.04).
key_findings.locator: Results, Psychopathology and correlations with metabolism (3.5.1)

key_findings.finding: The AMDP hallucinatory-disintegration subscale and schizophrenic syndrome score correlated negatively with the fronto-temporal and fronto-occipital ratio increases; the frontolateral-putamen ratio was the only cortical-subcortical ratio with a significant negative correlation with hallucinatory-disintegration in both hemispheres (left P<0.02, right P<0.001). The authors call this surprising and suggest that illusions and hallucinations relate more to occipital than to frontal change.
key_findings.locator: Table 2 (p. 33); Results (p. 34, 1st paragraph); Discussion, Hyperfrontality and psychopathology (p. 36)

key_findings.finding: Compared with published ego-pathology scores in people with first-episode schizophrenia, the (S)-ketamine scores for ego-consistency, ego-identity and ego-demarcation were about two-thirds of the patients' values, and the ego-activity and ego-vitality scores were clearly less affected; no patients were studied in this paper.

All participants recognised the (R)-ketamine condition as a drug effect and could tell it from the baseline (placebo) condition; the authors note that each had already received (S)-ketamine in a preliminary session held so that they could get used to lying still under the drug.
key_findings.locator: Materials and method, Phase I (2.5) (p. 28); Discussion, Psychopathology (p. 34); Discussion, Hyperfrontality and psychopathology (p. 36)

key_findings.finding: No correction was made for the number of comparisons, and the authors state that the results should be regarded as "exploratory rather than confirmatory".

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 prints a mean of 37.0 and an SD of 12.6 for the (S)-ketamine APZ global column, above which stand the ten per-person values 25, 47, 27, 37, 46, 27, 38, 33, 47 and 55. The editors' calculation from those ten values gives a mean of 38.2 and an SD of 10.3, and the printed pair is instead exactly the mean and SD of the racemic-ketamine APZ global column in Table 1 of the companion paper (p. 11 of Vollenweider et al. 1997b: 37.00 and 12.63), which lists a different set of ten people.
reporting_issues.consequence: The summary row for the paper's main psychopathological outcome appears to have been carried over from the companion study rather than computed from this study's data. The per-person values, not the summary row, should be used; all other columns of Table 1 reproduce correctly.

reporting_issues.issue: The column headed r(sp) in Table 2 holds P-levels with the sign of the correlation, not Spearman correlation coefficients, although the heading and the footnote both call them Spearman rho. The text confirms this: the frontolateral-putamen correlations with hallucinatory-disintegration are given there as P<0.02 (left) and P<0.001 (right), the same numbers printed in Table 2 as -0.02 and -0.001.
reporting_issues.consequence: A reader taking the table at face value would record correlations of about -0.001 to -0.08, that is essentially zero, where the authors mean significance levels with a direction. No correlation coefficient is printed anywhere in the paper, so the size of every symptom-metabolism association in this study is unknown and cannot be used in a claim.

reporting_issues.issue: The mean plasma level at the appearance of psychotic symptoms, 539 ng/ml, lies above the stated (S)-ketamine range of 269 to 523 ng/ml on the same page.
reporting_issues.consequence: Either the range describes per-person means of the five scan-period samples while 539 is an early induction-phase value, or one of the two is wrong; the paper does not say, so neither figure should be quoted as the concentration at which these effects occur.

reporting_issues.issue: The (S)-ketamine condition is described as 60% of the racemic amount used in the authors' earlier study, following a pilot potency ratio of about 1:0.6 mg/kg that is reported in one sentence with no sample size, no method and no reference. Editors' calculation from the two Methods sections (p. 26 here against p. 11 of Vollenweider et al. 1997b): the induction step is 75% of the companion study's (15 mg against 20 mg) and the maintenance rate 67-70% (0.014-0.02 against 0.02-0.03 mg/kg/min), but the maintenance phase here ran 53 min against 60 min, so the total amount over a session works out at about 61-64% for a person of 70 kg, close to the stated 60%.
reporting_issues.consequence: The stated ratio is consistent with the printed conditions once the shorter infusion is counted, so the objection to the conclusion that (S)-ketamine is the predominant psychotomimetic component of racemic ketamine (p. 34) is not arithmetic: it is that no racemic condition was given to these ten people, so the comparison is with a different sample in the companion paper, and that the pilot study behind the ratio is undescribed.

reporting_issues.issue: The third APZ subscale is labelled OSE where it should be VUS: the first subscale is introduced as OSE (oceanic boundlessness) and the third as OSE (visionary restructuralization), while the next sentence names the three dimensions OSE, AIA and VUS.
reporting_issues.consequence: A typographical slip, but it means the abbreviation OSE appears in the methods for two different subscales; all later uses of OSE in the results and discussion refer to oceanic boundlessness.

reporting_issues.issue: The text states that (S)-ketamine significantly increased the fronto-occipital ratios about 10% in both hemispheres, indicating a hyperfrontal pattern, but Table 2 marks both right-hemisphere fronto-occipital changes as not significant and the left frontomedial-occipitomedial change as trend level only; of the four, only the left frontolateral-occipitolateral change carries P<0.05.
reporting_issues.consequence: The hyperfrontality conclusion as drawn from the fronto-occipital ratios is weaker than the text states; the fronto-temporal ratios, which the table does mark significant in both hemispheres, carry most of the evidence.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract states that (S)-ketamine binds with a 3-4 times higher affinity to the PCP binding site than (R)-ketamine, while the Introduction gives 4 to 5 times, both citing the same source.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor, but the affinity ratio is the stated rationale for the dose choice and for the interpretation; neither figure should be quoted from this paper without going to the cited source.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 1 prints a mean age of 30.4 years and the text repeats it, above the ten ages 30, 40, 30, 42, 26, 24, 25, 34, 24 and 28, whose editors' calculation gives 30.3.
reporting_issues.consequence: Negligible for interpretation; recorded because it is the second arithmetic slip in the same table.

reporting_issues.issue: The dispersion shown in the psychopathology figures is stated two ways at once: the titles printed inside Figs. 1 and 2 give mean and standard deviation, and the captions of the same two figures open by saying mean and standard deviation and then state that the boxes indicate mean and standard error.
reporting_issues.consequence: These figures carry the only dispersion information for the AMDP, EWL and subscale scores, since no table prints them; with the two readings differing by a factor of about three for ten participants, nothing quantitative should be read off them.

reporting_issues.issue: The R-ketamine left frontomedial-temporolateral row of Table 2 carries a capital A as its P-level marker, where the footnote defines lower-case a as P<0.05 and lower-case b as P<0.01.
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical; read as P<0.05 by analogy with the rest of the table, but the paper does not define it.

reporting_issues.issue: The caption of Fig. 2 (p. 30) says that (S)-ketamine significantly increased the scores for 'emotional irritability' and 'anxiety', while the Results on p. 29 report four significant EWL scales: deactivation (P<0.01), introversion (P<0.05), emotional irritability (P<0.05) and anxiety (P<0.01).
reporting_issues.consequence: The figure is the only place the scale-by-scale mood data appear, and it disagrees with the text about how many mood scales changed; the Results' four scales should be used, with the disagreement stated.

verification.source_read: PDF PDFs/Ketamine/Vollenweider_1997a_SRKetaminePET.pdf, all 14 pages (pp. 25-38): full text, Tables 1 and 2, all five figures and their captions, acknowledgments and funding, plus the reference list. Tables 1 and 2 and the figures were checked on pages rendered at 150-400 dpi; no supplementary material exists.
verification.checked_by: AI reader 226 (blind second reading) and AI reader 231 (adjudication)

disagreements.first_pass: The (S)-ketamine condition is described as 60% of the racemic amount used in the authors' earlier study, following a pilot potency ratio of about 1:0.6 mg/kg, but the induction step here is 15 mg where the companion paper's is 20 mg, and the infusion rate here is 0.014-0.02 mg/kg/min where the companion paper's is higher (editors' comparison of the two Methods sections, p. 26 here against p. 11 of Vollenweider et al. 1997b: the ratios are about 70% and 75%, not 60%). | The claim that (S)-ketamine at 60% of a racemic amount produced virtually the same psychotic reactions (p. 34), and with it the inference that (S)-ketamine is the predominant psychotomimetic component of racemic ketamine, rests on a ratio that does not match the conditions as printed in the two papers.
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 226, corrected: the arithmetic is right but the consequence is too strong; counting the shorter 53-minute maintenance phase gives about 61-64% of the companion study's total at 70 kg, which is consistent with the stated 60%. What undercuts the inference is that no racemic condition was given to these ten people.
disagreements.resolution: Accepted after recomputing both schedules from the printed conditions (15 mg + 0.014-0.02 mg/kg/min for 53 min against 20 mg + 0.02-0.03 mg/kg/min for 60 min): 61.1% to 64.4% at 70 kg. The issue was rewritten so that it rests on the cross-sample comparison and on the undescribed pilot study, not on the ratio. The claim cl_ket_enantiomers was corrected to match.

disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 226, missed: Fig. 2's caption names two significant EWL scales where the Results name four.
disagreements.resolution: Confirmed on the rendered pp. 29 and 30 and added, because the figure is the only place the scale-by-scale data appear.

disagreements.first_pass: The 539 ng/ml at symptom onset lies above the top of the stated (S)-ketamine range of 269-523 ng/ml; the paper does not reconcile the two, and does not say whether the range refers to per-person means of the five samples.
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 226, missed: no molar calculation or concentration check is given for the equimolar claim; the measured plasma concentrations are the only evidence that the two conditions were comparable.
disagreements.resolution: Accepted and added to the note on the plasma-level finding, which is where the evidence sits.

disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 226, missed: the pilot study that fixed the (S) amount at 60% is given in one sentence (p. 26) with no sample size, method or reference, and appears to be unpublished.
disagreements.resolution: Accepted and folded into the rewritten reporting issue 3, where the equipotency premise belongs.
